Senses.Explanation: To hold fast and release is to pair restraint with letting something proceed. Xue'an Congjin and Shending Hongyin state the pair in their own addresses; an unnamed monk sets it aside while questioning Yuezhang Shoujing; Jiashan Shanhui places both actions under the holder's control. The pair names opposed actions, not a metaphysical formula.

To hold fast is to keep something firmly in hand or under control. Chan records characteristically load the verb against ‘release or let go’ (放行): the two can name opposed exercises of authority, yet Wansong also says each can operate inside the other, so neither word fixes one outcome by itself. The compound has 773 occurrences in 203 allowlisted storage files, and the contiguous pair ‘hold fast and release’ (把定放行) occurs 15 times in 13 texts. Wansong quotes the saying, ‘when held fast, true gold loses its color; when released, rubble shines’ (把定真金失色，放行瓦礫生光), and calls this ‘having capture and release, able to kill and bring to life’ (謂之有擒有縱，能殺能活). Xuedou preserves the same opposition: ‘when released, rubble shines; when held fast, true gold loses color; the authority is in hand, killing and bringing to life accord with the occasion’ (放行則瓦礫生光，把定則真金失色，權柄在手，殺活臨時). These lines contrast true gold and rubble under holding and release; they do not by themselves define gold as enlightenment or establish one symbolism for gold elsewhere. The common objects show the physical pressure retained by the verb: ‘hold heaven and earth fast’ (把定乾坤), ‘hold the world fast’ (把定世界), ‘hold the key crossing’ (把定要津), and ‘hold the throat’ (把定咽喉). Hongzhi calls ‘holding the throat’ the work of a good hand in commenting on an exchange. In a recorded question, Jiufeng is asked ‘what is the eye that holds heaven and earth fast?’ (如何是把定乾坤眼) and answers, ‘heaven and earth are inside it’ (乾坤在裏許), then identifies that as the heaven-and-earth eye (正是乾坤眼). Wansong elsewhere says one eye ‘is also called the eye that holds heaven and earth fast, continuously leaking not the slightest thread, and is also named the diamond eye at the crown’ (一隻眼又喚作把定乾坤眼，綿綿不漏絲毫，亦名頂門具金剛眼).
Senses.Note: The corpus uses the same verb for concrete grasping, for holding a passage or throat, and in the paired critical vocabulary ‘hold fast / release’ (把定／放行); these uses retain the literal opposition and do not require separate senses. Wansong further states, ‘where the ancients held fast, they could release and advance from the top of a pole; when releasing, they could hold firm, standing like a thousand-fathom wall’ (古人把定處放得行竿頭進步，放行時把得定壁立千仞). The record thus refuses a simple equation of holding with one fixed outcome; this entry reports the wording without assigning an intent to it.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes walk together hand in hand in these Chan records. Its wording is to take hands and walk together. Frozen-corpus concordance: 229 exact hits in 113 storage files representing 110 independent works. Chan records use it as a verdict of admitted company: the identified speaker says that whoever can inspect his statement may walk hand in hand south of Mount Sumeru, that one who can seize the snake safely may walk with the old monk, or that one commentator walks with Nanquan. Its companions range from buddhas and patriarchs to named masters and interlocutors who meet the stated test. Yuanwu's case commentary joins the phrase to entering mud and water together, living and dying together, making close participation in a public case—not generic companionship—the phrase's characteristic Chan deployment.

Senses.Explanation: To 把斷 is to hold something fast so that passage is completely blocked. Its characteristic Chan construction is 把斷要津, 'hold the strategic crossing shut': masters use it for command of the critical point, while monks quote it in public interviews to ask whether any way of helping or escaping remains. Verses make the same pressure concrete by saying the heavy crossing is barred and difficult to pass. The word names the blocking action, not a separate metaphysical gate.

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.

Senses.Explanation: A mosquito on an iron ox meets a surface on which its mouth has nowhere to enter. The stock completion repeatedly says “there is nowhere for you to put down your mouth.” Masters deploy it as an answer, a blocking verdict, and a description of an encounter in which verbal purchase is unavailable; one lineage story contrasts being like the mosquito at Shitou with a later breakthrough under Mazu.
